source.section: Schedule SB (PDF page 1) and its Instructions: line 16 and its Caution (SB Instructions PDF page 7; Publication 126 PDF page 8 section 4.E(1); Publication 106 PDF page 4 section 3.C(1)); Form 1 lines 1-12 (Form 1 PDF page 1); Form 1 Instructions PDF page 15 line 8 and lines 10a-10b (PDF pages 15-16), PDF pages 35-37 2025 Standard Deduction Table (row named in worked), PDF page 15 line 12 with the PDF pages 38-43 Tax Table and PDF page 44 Tax Computation Worksheet; tax figured from the 2025 Tax Rate Schedules, Publication 106 PDF pages 6-7

worked: Married filing jointly, you 67, spouse 60: you private pension 40,000; spouse wages 30,000. Only one spouse is 67: Wisconsin allows that spouse up to 24,000 (the 48,000 is only for a couple both 67), so the form's line 16 is 24,000. The projection applies the 48,000 joint cap to the 67-year-old's own income and subtracts all 40,000; expected follows the projection (accepted approximation). Federal (given, not tested): federal AGI = wages (spouse) 30,000.00 + private pension (you) 40,000.00 = 70,000.00. Federal taxable income = 70,000.00 - standard deduction 31,500.00 + 1 x 1,600.00 = 36,900.00; the federal senior deduction is ignored. Form 1 line 1 federal AGI 70,000.00; line 2 Schedule I adjustments 0.00; line 3 70,000.00; line 4 additions 0.00; line 5 70,000.00. Schedule SB: line 16 retirement income subtraction: qualifying income you (age 67): pension 40,000.00 = 40,000.00; smaller of 40,000.00 and the 48,000.00 cap = 40,000.00; line 50 total 40,000.00. Schedule SB line 17: federal AGI 70,000.00 is not less than 30,000.00, so no 5,000 subtraction. Form 1 line 6 40,000.00; line 7 Wisconsin income = 70,000.00 - 40,000.00 = 30,000.00. Line 8 standard deduction, 2025 Standard Deduction Table (Form 1 Instructions PDF page 35), row 30,000 to less than 30,500, column Married filing jointly: 24,707.00 (printed row, at least / less than / single / joint / separate / head of household: 30,000 / 30,500 / 12,276 / 24,707 / 8,595 / 15,111). Line 9 = 30,000.00 - 24,707.00 = 5,293.00. Line 10a 2 x 700 = 1,400.00; line 10b 1 x 250 = 250.00; line 10c 1,650.00. Line 11 taxable income = 5,293.00 - 1,650.00 = 3,643.00. Line 12 tax, Schedule B (joint) as numbers: 3.5% x 3,643.00 = 127.505; total 127.505, rounded once to 127.51. The Tax Table row 3,600 to 3,700 (PDF page 38) gives 128; expected keeps the schedule. Credits (lines 13-20, 30-35): none modelled; 0.00. State income tax 127.51. Form figure for comparison (line 16 24,000, the one-spouse cap): Form 1 line 6 24,000.00; line 7 Wisconsin income = 70,000.00 - 24,000.00 = 46,000.00. Line 8 standard deduction, 2025 Standard Deduction Table (Form 1 Instructions PDF page 35), row 46,000 to less than 46,500, column Married filing jointly: 21,542.00 (printed row, at least / less than / single / joint / separate / head of household: 46,000 / 46,500 / 10,356 / 21,542 / 5,431 / 11,508). Line 9 = 46,000.00 - 21,542.00 = 24,458.00. Line 10a 2 x 700 = 1,400.00; line 10b 1 x 250 = 250.00; line 10c 1,650.00. Line 11 taxable income = 24,458.00 - 1,650.00 = 22,808.00. Line 12 tax, Schedule B (joint) as numbers: 3.5% x 19,580.00 = 685.30 + 4.4% x 3,228.00 = 142.032; total 827.332, rounded once to 827.33. The Tax Table row 22,800 to 22,900 (PDF page 39) gives 829; expected keeps the schedule. Form state income tax 827.33. The projection's tax is 699.82 lower than the form's.
accepted_approximations: Joint return where only one spouse is 67 or older: the projection applies the 48,000 joint cap to that spouse's own qualifying income; Wisconsin allows 24,000 then (48,000 only when both are 67). A joint return where both are 67 is exact, which is why the joint cap is used.
The projection always takes the 24,000/48,000 subtraction for a person 67 or older, never the Wisconsin credits it bars (see not_modelled); a household whose credits are worth more would skip it.
